rows.stem: Choose the set of sex determining chromosomes that indicates the correct sex of the respective organism.

options.label: A
options.text: Homozygous sex chromosomes (ZZ) determine female sex in birds

options.label: B
options.text: XO type of sex chromosomes determine male sex in grasshoppers

options.label: C
options.text: XXY condition in humans, as found in Turner Syndrome, determines male sex

options.label: D
options.text: Homozygous sex chromosomes (XX) produce male sex in Drosophila

rows.solution:
- In birds the **female is heterogametic (ZW)** and the male is homogametic (ZZ), so ZZ determines a male, not a female.
- In grasshoppers the female has XX and the **male has a single X with no partner (XO)**, so the XO condition determines a male.
- XXY in humans is **Klinefelter's syndrome** and does give a male, but the option calls it Turner's syndrome, which is XO and gives a female; the pairing is wrong.
- In Drosophila, as in humans, XX determines a female and XY a male.

So the answer is option (B) XO type of sex chromosomes determine male sex in grasshoppers.

rows.stem:
Given below is a list of steps Meselson and Stahl carried out in their experiment to prove that DNA replication is semi-conservative. Select the option that gives the correct sequence of steps followed by them.
(i) Bacteria transferred to a \(\text{N}^{14}\) medium and sampled every 20 minutes.
(ii) All bacteria contain hybrid DNA (\(\text{N}^{14}\) DNA and \(\text{N}^{15}\) DNA).
(iii) Bacteria grown in \(\text{N}^{15}\) medium for many generations.
(iv) All bacteria contain \(\text{N}^{15}\) DNA.
(v) Bacteria contain either all \(\text{N}^{14}\) DNA or all hybrid DNA.
rows.solution: Meselson and Stahl first grew E. coli in a medium whose only nitrogen source was \(\text{N}^{15}\) for many generations (iii), so that all the bacteria carried heavy \(\text{N}^{15}\) DNA (iv). They then transferred the cells to a medium with normal \(\text{N}^{14}\) and took samples at definite intervals, as the cells divide every 20 minutes (i). After one generation all the DNA was **hybrid** (one \(\text{N}^{15}\) strand and one \(\text{N}^{14}\) strand) (ii), and after two generations the DNA was either light \(\text{N}^{14}\) DNA or hybrid DNA, in equal amounts (v). This is exactly what **semi-conservative replication** predicts. So the answer is option (C) (iii) \(\rightarrow\) (iv) \(\rightarrow\) (i) \(\rightarrow\) (ii) \(\rightarrow\) (v).

rows.stem: Identify the option that gives the correct type of evolution exhibited by the two animals shown, living in the same habitat in Australia.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:two line drawings side by side, separated by a vertical bar and captioned 'Mouse' (left) and 'Marsupial mouse' (right), both small long-tailed rodent-like animals; the stem names neither animal, so the captions carry what the question compares. Page idx 4.
rows.solution: The marsupial mouse of Australia and the placental mouse belong to two different lineages of mammals (pouched marsupials and placental mammals), yet they look alike because they occupy similar habitats and lead similar lives. When **different lineages come to resemble each other through adaptation to similar habitats**, the process is **convergent evolution**. The two animals are analogous, not homologous, in their resemblance. So the answer is option (A) Convergent Evolution.

rows.stem: A human male decides to adopt a surgical method for contraception. Identify the point in the diagram where a cut would be made and tied.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a line drawing of the human male reproductive system (testis and the ducts looping up over the bladder) with five pointer lines labelled S, T, Q, P and R from top to bottom; which structure each label marks is the whole question, so it is withheld here. Page idx 6.
rows.solution: The surgical method of contraception in the human male is **vasectomy**: a small part of the **vas deferens** is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum, so that sperms cannot pass from the testis to the urethra. In the diagram the label Q marks the vas deferens, the duct that runs up from the testis and loops over the urinary bladder. So the answer is option (C) Point Q.

rows.stem:
Which of the following options correctly matches the name of the hormone to its site of production in the human body ?
| Name of the Hormone | Site of Production |
|---|---|
| P. Oxytocin | i. Placenta |
| Q. Relaxin | ii. Corpus Luteum |
| R. hCG | iii. Pituitary Gland |
| S. Progesterone | iv. Ovaries |
rows.solution:
- Oxytocin is released from the **pituitary gland** (posterior pituitary) (iii).
- Relaxin is secreted by the **ovary** in the later phase of pregnancy (iv).
- hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) is produced by the **placenta** (i).
- Progesterone is secreted mainly by the **corpus luteum** (ii).

So the answer is option (C) P-iii, Q-iv, R-i, S-ii.

rows.stem: Which of the following seeds have remained alive for the longest period ?
rows.solution: Seeds of some species stay viable for very long periods. The oldest viable seed on record is of the lupine (Lupinus arcticus), excavated from the Arctic tundra, about 10,000 years old; it is not among the choices. Among those given, the record belongs to the **date palm, Phoenix dactylifera**: a seed about 2000 years old, recovered during archaeological excavation at King Herod's palace near the Dead Sea, germinated. So the answer is option (A) Phoenix dactylifera.

rows.stem:
Select the options which is/are incorrect statement(s) with respect to T-lymphocytes in the human body.
(i) They are a type of white blood cells.
(ii) They are produced in bone marrow.
(iii) They remain active at all times in the body.
(iv) They mature in the bone marrow.
rows.solution:
CBSE accepted both '(iii) only' and '(iii) and (iv) only' for this question.

- (i) T-lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell (a lymphocyte), so the statement is correct.
- (ii) Like all lymphocytes they are produced in the **bone marrow**, so the statement is correct.
- (iii) They do not remain active all the time; they are activated only when they meet their specific antigen, and memory T-cells then stay ready for a later encounter. The statement is incorrect.
- (iv) T-lymphocytes **mature in the thymus**, not in the bone marrow (B-lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow). The statement is incorrect.

So the incorrect statements are (iii) and (iv). So the answer is option (D) (iii) and (iv) only.

rows.stem:
Human settlement often leads to habitat loss which leads to fragmentation, forming smaller patches of habitats. Select the statements that describe how a small patch differs from a large patch of the same habitat.
(i) Invasive species will never be seen here.
(ii) Population of large animals decreases.
(iii) Biodiversity decreases.
(iv) Competition from surrounding habitats increases.
Identify the option that does not exhibit a parasitic relationship.
rows.solution: A parasite lives on or in a host for a long time and draws its nourishment from it: head lice and ticks are ectoparasites feeding on the blood of their hosts, and Cuscuta is a parasitic plant that draws nutrients from the host tree through haustoria. The female Anopheles mosquito only visits a human to take a blood meal and then leaves; it does not live on the host, and it acts as the **vector** that transmits the malarial parasite, Plasmodium. So it does not exhibit a parasitic relationship. So the answer is option (C) Female Anopheles.

rows.stem: Identify the fungus that ripens the famous 'Roquefort' cheese :
rows.solution:
CBSE awarded the mark to every student who attempted this question, because none of the options is correct.

The famous 'Roquefort' cheese is ripened by growing a specific fungus on it, **Penicillium roqueforti**, which gives the cheese its particular flavour. None of the four organisms listed does this. Penicillium notatum is the mould from which Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, Saccharomyces cerevisiae is baker's and brewer's yeast, Propionibacterium sharmanii is the bacterium whose carbon dioxide makes the large holes in Swiss cheese, and Monascus purpureus is the yeast that produces statins. So no choice names the fungus of Roquefort cheese.

rows.subtopic: Isolation, Cutting and Amplification of DNA
rows.stem:
The given schematic illustration shows three steps 'P', 'Q' and 'R' of the polymerase chain reaction.
Which of the following statements are correct with reference to the illustration given above ?
(i) Step 'P' is showing denaturation at low temperature.
(ii) Step 'Q' is a denaturation of DNA strand at high temperature, followed by annealing.
(iii) Step 'R' is an extension of DNA in presence of thermostable DNA polymerase.
(iv) Step 'Q' is extension with two sets of primers.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:three DNA schematics stacked and labelled Step 'P', Step 'Q' and Step 'R', each strand with its 5' and 3' ends marked and a hatched region on the strands; what each step's drawing shows (strands paired or separated, short or full-length hatched segments) is what the statements are judged against, so it is withheld here. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
The three drawings follow the steps of one PCR cycle.
- Step 'P' shows the double-stranded template DNA with the region to be amplified; this is the starting DNA, and denaturation is done at a **high** temperature, not a low one. Statement (i) is incorrect.
- Step 'Q' shows the two strands separated (**denaturation** at high temperature) with short primers bound to each strand at the ends of the target region (**annealing**). Statement (ii) is correct, and statement (iv), which calls this step extension, is incorrect.
- Step 'R' shows each primer lengthened along the whole target region: this is **extension**, carried out by a thermostable DNA polymerase such as Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus. Statement (iii) is correct.

So the answer is option (B) (ii) and (iii) only.

rows.stem: DNA profiles of the child and three individuals 1, 2 and 3 who claim to be the parents of the child are given below. Select the option that shows the correct actual parent/parents of the child.

options.label: D
options.text: Individual 1 is the only parent of the child amongst 1, 2 and 3

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a boxed gel of four lanes of DNA bands headed Child X, Individual 1, Individual 2 and Individual 3; which individuals' bands account for the child's is the answer, so the band positions are withheld here. Page idx 12.
rows.solution: A child inherits half of its DNA from each biological parent, so every band in the child's DNA profile must be present in the profile of one parent or the other. Comparing the lanes, each band of child X matches a band of individual 1 or of individual 3, and the two together account for all of the child's bands; several of the child's bands have no match in individual 2. So individuals 1 and 3 are the actual parents. So the answer is option (A) Individual 1 and 3.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : In humans the genotype with all the dominant alleles (AABBCC) will have the darkest skin colour.
Reason (R) : In a polygenic trait, phenotype reflects the contribution of each allele.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Human skin colour is a **polygenic trait**, controlled by three genes, A, B and C, whose dominant alleles each add to the amount of melanin. The phenotype therefore reflects the contribution of every allele: the more dominant alleles a genotype carries, the darker the skin. So AABBCC, with all six dominant alleles, has the darkest skin, and aabbcc the lightest. Both statements are true and the Reason explains the Assertion. So both the Assertion and the Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The number of white winged moths decreased drastically after industrialisation in England.
Reason (R) : Effects of industrialisation were more marked in rural areas of England.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: In England, before industrialisation, white-winged moths outnumbered dark-winged moths, because white moths resting on lichen-covered tree trunks were hidden from predators. After industrialisation, smoke and soot killed the lichens and darkened the tree trunks, so white moths were picked off by birds and their numbers fell drastically, while dark moths survived. The Assertion is true. But these effects were marked in the **industrial (urban) areas**; in rural areas, where there was less industry, the white moths remained common. The Reason is false. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : More and more children in metro cities of India suffer from allergies and asthma due to sensitivity to the environment.
Reason (R) : Modern day lifestyle and a protected environment in early life has resulted in lowering the immunity.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: An **allergy** is the exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens in the environment (allergens) such as dust, pollen and mites. The use of drugs like anti-histamines and steroids reduces the symptoms. The increase in allergies and asthma among children in metro cities is attributed to sensitivity to the environment, which results from the modern lifestyle and a protected environment in early life that lowers the immunity. Both statements are true and the Reason explains the Assertion. So both the Assertion and the Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys uses sexual deceit to get pollinated by a species of bee.
Reason (R) : The female bee changes its colour depending on the temperature of the area.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys uses **sexual deceit**: one petal of its flower bears an uncanny resemblance to the female of a bee species in size, colour and markings. The male bee is attracted to what it perceives as a female, 'pseudocopulates' with the flower, and is dusted with pollen, which it transfers to the next flower. The Assertion is true. The female bee does not change its colour with temperature; the point of the example is **co-evolution**: if the female bee's colour pattern changes even slightly during evolution, pollination success falls unless the orchid's petal co-evolves to keep the resemblance. The Reason is false. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem:
(a) Explain the process of the development of a male gametophyte in an angiosperm.
(b) Why is it called a male gametophyte ?
rows.solution:
(a) Development of the male gametophyte:
- Each cell of the **sporogenous tissue** in the microsporangium of the anther acts as a **pollen mother cell (microspore mother cell)**.
- It undergoes **meiosis** to form a cluster of four haploid cells, the **microspore tetrad** (microsporogenesis).
- As the anther matures and dehydrates, the microspores dissociate from one another and develop into **pollen grains**.
- In the mature pollen grain the cell divides by mitosis into a large **vegetative cell** and a small **generative cell**; pollen is shed at this two-celled stage in most angiosperms, and in others at a three-celled stage.

(b) The pollen grain is the haploid, gamete-producing generation of the plant: its **generative cell divides mitotically to form the two male gametes**. Because it carries and produces the male gametes, it is called the male gametophyte.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the first step the primary effluent undergoes when it enters the secondary treatment plant and state the purpose.
(b) What is the level of B.O.D indicative of in the secondary treatment plant ? Mention its significance.
rows.solution:
(a) The primary effluent is passed into large **aeration tanks**, where it is constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped into it. This allows vigorous growth of useful aerobic microbes into **flocs** (masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments to form mesh-like structures). The purpose is that these microbes consume the major part of the organic matter in the effluent, which significantly **reduces the BOD** of the effluent.

(b) BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) is the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria. It is therefore a **measure of the organic matter in the water**: the greater the BOD of waste water, the greater its polluting potential. Its significance in the plant is that the sewage water is treated until the BOD is reduced significantly; only then is the effluent passed into the settling tank and on towards release.

rows.stem:
Given below is a food web that involves nine organisms.
(a) Identify two producers and two carnivores shown in the food web.
(b) Is it possible to make an ecological pyramid depicting this food web ? Give reason in support of your answer.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a food web of nine organisms numbered 1 to 9, with 1, 2 and 3 on the bottom row, 4 and 5 above them, 6, 7 and 8 above those and 9 at the top, joined by arrows; which numbers feed on which is the whole of part (a), so the arrows are withheld here. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
CBSE accepted either answer to part (b), "no" or "yes", provided it was supported by the matching reason.

(a) **Producers** are the organisms that no arrow enters, because they make their own food: organisms **1, 2 and 3**. Organisms 4 and 5 eat the producers, so they are herbivores (primary consumers). **Carnivores** are the organisms that feed on other animals: **6, 7 and 8**, which feed on the herbivores 4 and 5, and **9**, which feeds on 6 and 8. Any two of 1, 2, 3 and any two of 6, 7, 8, 9 are correct.

(b) No. An ecological pyramid is built for a food **chain**: it assumes a simple chain in which each organism occupies one trophic level, so it **does not accommodate a food web**, where organisms are interconnected and an organism may feed at more than one level. Alternatively, yes: in this particular web **no organism occupies more than one trophic level** (1-3 are producers, 4-5 herbivores, 6-8 first-level carnivores and 9 a top carnivore), so the organisms can be grouped level by level into a pyramid.

rows.stem: Illustrate with the help of an example how introduction of an alien species turns invasive and causes decline of an indigenous species.
rows.solution:
When an alien species is introduced into a new habitat, it often meets no natural predators or competitors there, so it multiplies unchecked, becomes **invasive** and drives native species to decline or extinction.

Example: the **Nile perch** was introduced into **Lake Victoria** in East Africa. Being a large predatory fish, it fed on the native **cichlid fish** and eventually led to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlids in the lake.

Other examples: the illegal introduction of the African catfish, Clarias gariepinus, for aquaculture threatens the indigenous catfishes of Indian rivers; carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) have spread and threaten native plant species.

rows.stem: 'Insertional inactivation' is a method to detect recombinant DNA. Explain the method.
rows.solution:
In insertional inactivation, the recombinant DNA (the desired DNA) is inserted within the coding sequence of the enzyme **\(\beta\)-galactosidase** in the vector. This **inactivates the gene** for the enzyme, so a recombinant cannot make \(\beta\)-galactosidase.

The bacteria are then grown on a medium containing a **chromogenic substrate**:
- colonies whose plasmid has **no insert** (non-recombinants) still make the enzyme, which acts on the substrate and gives **blue-coloured colonies**;
- colonies whose plasmid **carries the insert** (recombinants) cannot make the enzyme and give **colourless colonies**.

So the recombinant colonies are identified simply by their lack of colour. This is a simpler procedure than selecting on two antibiotics, which needs replica plating.

rows.stem: Explain how recombinant DNA technology is used to detect a disease even before any clinical symptom appears.
rows.solution:
A disease is normally detected after its symptoms appear, by which time the pathogen or the mutated gene is present in large amounts. Recombinant DNA technology allows **early diagnosis**:
- **PCR (polymerase chain reaction)**: the very small amount of the pathogen's DNA or RNA present in a patient's sample is **amplified** many times by repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing of pathogen-specific primers and extension, so it can be detected. PCR is routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients and to detect mutations in genes in suspected cancer patients.
- **Probe and autoradiography**: a single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule (a **probe**) is allowed to hybridise with its complementary DNA in a clone of cells, and the clone is detected by **autoradiography**. A clone carrying a mutated gene will not appear on the photographic film, because the probe is not complementary to the mutated gene.

rows.stem:
(i) How many types of RNA polymerases are there in a eukaryote cell ? Mention which one of them transcribes hnRNA.
(ii) Write the changes that hnRNA undergoes before it leaves the nucleus as mRNA.
rows.solution:
(i) There are **three types of RNA polymerases** in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell:
- RNA polymerase I transcribes the rRNAs (28S, 18S and 5.8S);
- RNA polymerase II transcribes the precursor of mRNA, the **heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA)**;
- RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs.
So hnRNA is transcribed by **RNA polymerase II**.

(ii) Before it leaves the nucleus as mRNA, the hnRNA undergoes three changes:
- **Splicing**: the introns (non-coding sequences) are removed and the exons are joined in a definite order.
- **Capping**: an unusual nucleotide, methyl guanosine triphosphate, is added to the 5'-end of the hnRNA.
- **Tailing**: adenylate residues (200-300) are added at the 3'-end in a template-independent manner.
The fully processed hnRNA, now called mRNA, is transported out of the nucleus for translation.

rows.stem: The length of DNA in any cell is far greater than the dimension of its nucleus. Explain how this enormous DNA is packaged in a eukaryotic cell.
rows.solution:
The length of DNA is enormous: a human diploid cell has \(6.6 \times 10^{9}\) bp, and since the distance between two consecutive base pairs is \(0.34 \times 10^{-9}\) m, the DNA is about \(6.6 \times 10^{9} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9} = 2.2\) metres long, far greater than a typical nucleus (about \(10^{-6}\) m). It is packaged as follows:
- DNA is negatively charged. A set of **positively charged basic proteins, the histones**, rich in the basic amino acid residues **lysine and arginine**, holds it.
- Eight histone molecules organise into a unit called the **histone octamer**.
- The negatively charged DNA is wrapped around the positively charged histone octamer to form a structure called the **nucleosome**. A typical nucleosome contains **200 bp** of DNA helix.
- Nucleosomes are the repeating units of a structure in the nucleus called **chromatin**, the thread-like stained bodies seen in the nucleus; under the electron microscope they appear as **'beads-on-string'**.
- The beads-on-string chromatin is further packaged into chromatin fibres, which coil and condense at metaphase to form chromosomes. This higher-level packaging needs an additional set of proteins, the **non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins**.

rows.stem:
Expand and explain the following techniques used in the 'Test Tube Baby' programme :
(a) GIFT
(b) ZIFT
(c) IUI
rows.solution:
Strictly, only ZIFT among these three involves fertilisation outside the body (in vitro), so CBSE also credited a student who wrote that GIFT and IUI have no role in a test tube baby programme. Each technique is explained below.

(a) **GIFT: Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer.** An ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of another female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and further development. Fertilisation then takes place inside her body.

(b) **ZIFT: Zygote Intra Fallopian Transfer.** Ova from the wife or a donor and sperms from the husband or a donor are fused in the laboratory (in vitro fertilisation), and the zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the **fallopian tube**. (An embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus instead: IUT.)

(c) **IUI: Intra Uterine Insemination.** Semen collected either from the husband or from a healthy donor is artificially introduced into the vagina or into the **uterus** of the female. It is used where the male partner cannot inseminate the female or has a very low sperm count.

rows.stem:
Given below is a diagrammatic sectional view of a seminiferous tubule. State the developmental process of :
(a) (i) 'b' from 'a'.
(ii) 'e' from 'd'.
(iii) 'd' from 'b'.
(b) Identify 'a', 'b' and 'c'.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a coloured sectional view of part of a seminiferous tubule, layers of rounded cells resting on a basal layer with tailed sperms at the lumen side, and five pointer lines labelled a, b, c, d and e; which cell each label marks is what both parts ask, so it is withheld here. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(a)
(i) 'b' (the **secondary spermatocyte**) is formed from 'a' (the **primary spermatocyte**) by the **first meiotic division (meiosis I)**, a reduction division: each diploid primary spermatocyte gives two equal, haploid secondary spermatocytes.
(ii) 'e' (the **sperm**) is formed from 'd' (the **spermatid**) by **spermiogenesis**, the differentiation of a spermatid into a sperm. The sperm heads stay embedded in the Sertoli cells until they are released from the tubule (spermiation).
(iii) 'd' (the **spermatids**) are formed from 'b' (the secondary spermatocytes) by the **second meiotic division (meiosis II)**, which gives four haploid spermatids from each primary spermatocyte.

(b)
- a: primary spermatocyte
- b: secondary spermatocyte
- c: Sertoli cell, which provides nutrition to the germ cells

rows.stem:
(a) Darwin's theory of Natural Selection is widely accepted but some limitations have been identified by modern biologists. Mention the limitations identified.
(b) Name and state the most accepted theory of evolution in modern times.
(c) Mention any two ways the limitations identified in Darwin's theory of evolution are explained in modern biology.

(a) Name the category of drugs represented by the chemical structure given above.
(b) If the methyl group is substituted by acetyl group we get a bitter crystalline compound. Name the compound.
(c) Name the natural source of these compounds.
(d) State the harmful effects of this class of drugs on the human body.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a drawn chemical structure printed above the parts, with no caption: a fused ring system carrying two HO groups, an O bridge, an H on a wedge and an N bearing a CH3 group. The stem names no compound and naming it would answer part (a), so it is described and not named here. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
(a) The structure is that of **morphine**, so it represents the **opioids**, drugs that bind to specific opioid receptors present in the central nervous system and the gastro-intestinal tract.

(b) The compound is **heroin**, commonly called **smack**, chemically **diacetylmorphine**. It is a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound.

(c) The natural source is the latex of the **poppy plant, Papaver somniferum**, from which morphine is extracted; heroin is obtained by acetylation of morphine.

(d) Heroin and the other opioids are **depressants**: they **slow down body functions**. Taken repeatedly, they cause tolerance and dependence (addiction), with withdrawal symptoms when the drug is stopped, and taken intravenously they carry the risk of AIDS and hepatitis B through shared needles.

Note: heroin is made by attaching acetyl groups to the two -OH groups of morphine, which is why it is called diacetylmorphine; the methyl group on the nitrogen stays in place. The question's wording, "the methyl group is substituted by acetyl group", is loose, but the compound it points to is heroin.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the scientific name of the nematode that infests the tobacco plants and the part that it infests.
(b) How is Agrobacterium used to protect tobacco plant from this attack ?
rows.solution:
(a) The nematode is **Meloidogyne incognita**. It infects the **roots** of tobacco plants and causes a great reduction in yield.

(b) Agrobacterium is used as a **vector** to introduce nematode-specific genes into the tobacco plant, which then protects itself by **RNA interference (RNAi)**:
- Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes are introduced into the host plant.
- The introduced DNA is arranged so that it produces both **sense and anti-sense RNA** in the host cells.
- These two RNAs, being complementary to each other, form a **double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)** that initiates RNAi.
- RNAi silences the specific mRNA of the nematode, so the parasite cannot survive in a transgenic host expressing the specific interfering RNA. The transgenic plant thus protects itself from the parasite.

rows.stem:
Explain the following population interactions with the help of one example each :
(a) Brood Parasitism
(b) Co-evolution of mutualists
rows.solution:
(a) **Brood parasitism** is a form of parasitism in birds in which the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of its host and lets the host incubate them. During evolution the eggs of the parasitic bird have come to **resemble the host's eggs** in size and colour, which reduces the chance of the host detecting the foreign eggs and ejecting them from the nest. Example: the **cuckoo (koel)** lays its eggs in the nest of the **crow**, and the crow hatches and raises the young.

(b) **Co-evolution of mutualists**: in a mutualistic interaction the evolution of one species is tightly linked with the evolution of its partner, so the two evolve together. Example: **fig trees and fig wasps**. Each fig species is pollinated only by its 'partner' wasp species. The female wasp uses the fig fruit both as an oviposition site and uses the developing seeds within it to nourish its larvae, and in doing so it pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for suitable egg-laying sites. The fig in turn offers the wasp some of its developing seeds as food for the larvae.

rows.stem: Is the disease sex-linked or autosomal as per the chart ? Give reasons in support of your answer.
rows.context: The following pedigree chart shows the inheritance of a genetic disorder up to three generations of a family. Observe the chart and answer the questions that follow.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a three-generation pedigree of circles (females) and squares (males) with every individual lettered: Generation I 'B' and 'A' as a couple; Generation II their children 'C', 'D' and 'E', with 'E' married to 'F'; Generation III the children of 'E' and 'F', namely 'G', 'H' and 'I'. Which symbols are shaded decides every sub-part, so it is withheld here. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
According to the chart the disease is **sex-linked** (X-linked). The reason: **only males are affected** in the family (the father in generation I, his son in generation II and that son's son in generation III). A male has only one X chromosome, so a recessive allele on his X is always expressed, whereas a female with one such allele is protected by the normal allele on her other X; this is why such disorders show up far more often in males.

Note: the chart can also be read as autosomal recessive, and on the sex-linked reading the two unaffected wives 'B' and 'F' must both be carriers, because a father passes his Y chromosome, not his X, to his son. The marking scheme takes the sex-linked reading, which the later parts of this question also assume.

rows.stem: Is it a recessive or a dominant disorder ?
rows.context: The following pedigree chart shows the inheritance of a genetic disorder up to three generations of a family. Observe the chart and answer the questions that follow.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's three-generation pedigree of lettered individuals 'A' to 'I'; which symbols are shaded decides the answer, so it is withheld here. Page idx 24.
rows.solution: It is a **recessive** disorder. The affected son 'E' is born to an unaffected mother, and the affected son 'I' to an unaffected mother too, so the allele is carried without being expressed. Also, a dominant X-linked disorder in the father 'A' would have appeared in all his daughters, yet his daughters 'C' and 'D' are unaffected.

rows.stem: Write the genotypes of the individuals 'C', 'D' and 'H'.
rows.context: The following pedigree chart shows the inheritance of a genetic disorder up to three generations of a family. Observe the chart and answer the questions that follow.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's three-generation pedigree of lettered individuals 'A' to 'I'; who is shaded and who the parents of 'C', 'D' and 'H' are decides the genotypes, so the shading is withheld here. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
Using \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\) for the X chromosome carrying the affected allele:
- 'C' and 'D' are unaffected daughters of the affected father 'A', so each has received his \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\): both are carriers, \(\text{XX}^{\text{c}}\).
- 'H' is an unaffected daughter of the affected father 'E', so she too has received his \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\): she is a carrier, \(\text{XX}^{\text{c}}\).

So C: \(\text{XX}^{\text{c}}\), D: \(\text{XX}^{\text{c}}\), H: \(\text{XX}^{\text{c}}\).

rows.stem: If the female 'D' marries a normal man, what will be the probability of their daughter being a sufferer of this disease ?
rows.context: The following pedigree chart shows the inheritance of a genetic disorder up to three generations of a family. Observe the chart and answer the questions that follow.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's three-generation pedigree of lettered individuals 'A' to 'I'; the genotype of 'D' follows from the shading of her parents, which is withheld here. Page idx 24.
rows.solution: 'D' is a carrier, \(\text{XX}^{\text{c}}\), and a normal man is \(\text{XY}\). Every daughter receives her father's normal X, so a daughter is either \(\text{XX}\) (normal) or \(\text{XX}^{\text{c}}\) (carrier), and none can be \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{X}^{\text{c}}\). So the probability of their daughter being a sufferer is **0%** (half the daughters will be carriers).

rows.stem: If the mother 'B' is a carrier of the disease, what will be the probability of their daughter being a sufferer of this disease ?
rows.context: The following pedigree chart shows the inheritance of a genetic disorder up to three generations of a family. Observe the chart and answer the questions that follow.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's three-generation pedigree of lettered individuals 'A' to 'I'; whether the father 'A' is affected is in the shading, which is withheld here. Page idx 24.
rows.solution: If the mother 'B' is a carrier, \(\text{XX}^{\text{c}}\), and the father 'A' is affected, \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{Y}\), every daughter receives the father's \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\), and from the mother either X or \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\) with equal chance. So half the daughters are \(\text{XX}^{\text{c}}\) (carriers) and half are \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{X}^{\text{c}}\) (affected). The probability of their daughter being a sufferer is **50%**.

rows.stem: Name the parasitic stage that is being transferred from host 'X' to host 'Y'.
rows.context: The diagram shows the life cycle of a pathogenic protozoan.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a life-cycle cycle diagram with two blobs labelled Host 'X' and Host 'Y' joined by two curved arrows labelled 'A' and 'B', each annotated with a mosquito-bite caption; from Host 'Y' an arrow 'C' leads to a circle 'infects the liver', then an arrow 'D' to an RBC holding small bodies, and an arrow from the RBC back to Host 'Y'. Which host is the mosquito and which the human is carried by the captions and arrow directions, so they are withheld here. Page idx 26.
rows.solution: The diagram is the life cycle of Plasmodium, the malarial parasite: host 'X' is the female Anopheles mosquito and host 'Y' is the human. The stage transferred from the mosquito to the human, when an infected female Anopheles bites, is the **sporozoite**, the infectious form of the parasite.

rows.stem: Write the changes the parasite undergoes in the liver.
rows.context: The diagram shows the life cycle of a pathogenic protozoan.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's life-cycle diagram of Host 'X', Host 'Y', the liver and an RBC joined by arrows 'A' to 'D'; it names the vector, which identifies the protozoan the context leaves unnamed. Page idx 26.
rows.solution: In the liver the sporozoites enter the liver cells and **multiply asexually**, producing large numbers of the parasite, which are then released into the blood and attack the red blood cells.

rows.stem: Write the changes the parasite undergoes when it enters the RBC.
rows.context: The diagram shows the life cycle of a pathogenic protozoan.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's life-cycle diagram of Host 'X', Host 'Y', the liver and an RBC joined by arrows 'A' to 'D'; it names the vector, which identifies the protozoan the context leaves unnamed. Page idx 26.
rows.solution: In the RBCs the parasites **multiply asexually** again, and the infected RBCs rupture, releasing parasites that infect fresh RBCs. Some of the parasites in the RBCs then **develop into gametocytes** (the sexual stages), which are ready to be taken up by a mosquito.

rows.stem: Trace the changes the parasite undergoes when the host 'X' takes its blood meal from infected host 'Y'.
rows.context: The diagram shows the life cycle of a pathogenic protozoan.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's life-cycle diagram of Host 'X', Host 'Y', the liver and an RBC joined by arrows 'A' to 'D'; it names the vector, which identifies the protozoan the context leaves unnamed. Page idx 26.
rows.solution: When the female Anopheles (host 'X') takes a blood meal from an infected human (host 'Y'), it takes up the **gametocytes** with the blood. In the mosquito's stomach the gametocytes develop into **gametes**, **fertilisation** takes place and the zygote develops further in the stomach wall. The parasites multiply to form **sporozoites**, which move to the mosquito's **salivary glands**, ready to be injected into the next human the mosquito bites.

rows.stem: At which stage during the life cycle of the pathogen does the host 'Y' experience the symptoms of the disease ? Name the disease and the toxic substance responsible for these symptoms.
rows.context: The diagram shows the life cycle of a pathogenic protozoan.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's life-cycle diagram of Host 'X', Host 'Y', the liver and an RBC joined by arrows 'A' to 'D'; it names the vector, which identifies the disease the stem asks for. Page idx 26.
rows.solution: The human (host 'Y') experiences the symptoms when the infected **RBCs rupture**. The disease is **malaria**, and the rupture of RBCs releases a toxic substance, **haemozoin**, which is responsible for the chill and high fever recurring every three to four days.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions with respect to recombinant DNA technology :
(i) Why is plasmid considered to be an important tool in rDNA technology ? From where can plasmids be isolated ? (Any two sources)
(ii) Explain the role of 'ori' and selectable marker in a cloning vector.
(iii) "r-DNA technology cannot proceed without restriction endonuclease." Justify.

Answer the following questions based on Bt-crops :
(i) Why do farmers prefer to grow Bt cotton crop than genetically unmodified cotton crops ?
(ii) Name any two insects that are killed by Bt toxin.
(iii) Explain the mechanism by which Bt toxin kills the insects but not the bacterium which possesses the toxin.
rows.solution:
(i) Bt cotton is a transgenic crop carrying a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, so the plant itself makes an insecticidal protein and is **resistant to insect pests** such as the cotton bollworm. Farmers prefer it because it **reduces the use of chemical insecticides**, cuts the cost of cultivation and the damage to the environment, and gives a **higher yield**.

(ii) Insects killed by Bt toxin (any two): **cotton bollworm**, **corn borer**, tobacco budworm and armyworm (lepidopterans); beetles (coleopterans); flies and mosquitoes (dipterans).

(iii) Mechanism:
- Bacillus thuringiensis forms protein crystals containing a toxic insecticidal protein. In the bacterium the Bt toxin exists as an **inactive protoxin**, so the bacterium itself is not harmed.
- When an insect eats the plant, the inactive toxin is converted into the **active form** because the **alkaline pH of the insect gut** solubilises the crystals.
- The activated toxin binds to the surface of the **midgut epithelial cells** and creates **pores** in them.
- The cells swell and lyse, and eventually the insect dies.

The toxin is coded by genes named cry; the proteins encoded by cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworms, and that of cryIAb controls the corn borer.

rows.stem: Protein synthesis requires the services of all three types of RNAs, namely t-RNA, m-RNA and r-RNA. Explain the role of each of them during the process of protein synthesis in prokaryotes.
rows.solution:
In translation the three types of RNA work together.

**mRNA (messenger RNA): the template.**
- It carries the genetic information from DNA in the form of **codons**, triplets of bases, each coding for one amino acid; the sequence of codons decides the sequence of amino acids in the protein.
- It carries the **start (initiator) codon AUG**, at which translation begins, and the **stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA**, at which it ends. The stretch between them is the translational unit, and untranslated regions (UTRs) on either side help efficient translation.

**tRNA (transfer RNA): the adapter.**
- It has an **anticodon loop** whose bases are complementary to a codon on the mRNA, and an **amino acid acceptor end** to which its specific amino acid binds.
- Amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their tRNA (charging, or aminoacylation of tRNA). The tRNA then reads the code and brings the specific amino acid to the ribosome, so it acts as the adapter between the code and the amino acid. A special **initiator tRNA** starts the process.

**rRNA (ribosomal RNA): the machinery and the catalyst.**
- rRNA, with proteins, organises the **ribosome**, the cellular factory of protein synthesis, with a large and a small subunit.
- Translation begins when the **small subunit encounters the mRNA**. The large subunit has **two sites** where the incoming charged tRNAs bind, so that two amino acids are brought close enough for a peptide bond to form.
- The ribosome also acts as the **catalyst for peptide bond formation**: in bacteria, the 23S rRNA is the enzyme, a ribozyme.

The ribosome moves from codon to codon along the mRNA, adding amino acids one by one, until it reaches a stop codon, where a release factor binds and the complete polypeptide is released from the ribosome.

rows.stem:
A homozygous tall pea plant with green seeds is crossed with a homozygous dwarf pea plant with yellow seeds.
(i) Write the possible phenotype and genotype of \(\text{F}_1\) generation.
(ii) State the laws of Mendel that are proved true by the \(\text{F}_1\) generation.
(iii) Mention the \(\text{F}_2\) phenotypic ratio along with their possible phenotypes.
(iv) Write the genotypes of the male and female gametes produced by \(\text{F}_1\) progeny.
rows.solution:
Let T stand for tall and t for dwarf, and Y for yellow seed and y for green seed (yellow is dominant over green). The tall green parent is TTyy and the dwarf yellow parent is ttYY.

(i) The tall parent gives gametes Ty and the dwarf parent gives tY, so every \(\text{F}_1\) plant has the genotype **TtYy** and the phenotype **tall plant with yellow seeds**.

(ii) The \(\text{F}_1\) generation proves:
- the **Law of Dominance**: of a pair of contrasting characters, only one (the dominant: tall, yellow) appears in the \(\text{F}_1\) hybrid, while the other (the recessive: dwarf, green) remains unexpressed, although its factor is present;
- the **Law of Segregation**: in the hybrid the two alleles of a pair (T and t, Y and y) remain together without blending, and they separate (segregate) at the time of gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one allele of each pair. The reappearance of the recessive dwarf and green characters in the \(\text{F}_2\) confirms it.

(iii) Selfing the \(\text{F}_1\) gives the \(\text{F}_2\) phenotypes in the ratio **9 : 3 : 3 : 1**: 9 tall yellow : 3 tall green : 3 dwarf yellow : 1 dwarf green.

(iv) Since the two genes assort independently, each \(\text{F}_1\) plant (TtYy) produces four kinds of gametes in equal proportion:
- male gametes: TY, Ty, tY, ty;
- female gametes: TY, Ty, tY, ty.

rows.stem:
(i) Double fertilisation is an event unique to all flowering plants. Explain the process.
(ii) Give a reason for the following :
(1) A seed of an orange has many embryos.
(2) Cashew is a false fruit but Guava is a true fruit.
rows.solution:
(i) **Double fertilisation** is the occurrence of **two types of fusion, syngamy and triple fusion, in one embryo sac**, and it is unique to flowering plants.
- The pollen tube enters one of the synergids and releases the **two male gametes** into its cytoplasm.
- **Syngamy**: one male gamete moves towards the egg cell and fuses with its nucleus, forming the **diploid zygote**, which develops into the embryo.
- **Triple fusion**: the other male gamete moves towards the two polar nuclei in the central cell and fuses with them, producing a **triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)**. The central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell, which develops into the endosperm that nourishes the embryo.

(ii)
(1) Orange seeds show **polyembryony**. Some of the **nucellar cells** surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos. So each seed contains several embryos, besides the one formed from the zygote.
(2) A true fruit develops only from the ovary after fertilisation, while in a false fruit other floral parts also contribute. In **cashew**, the **thalamus** also contributes to fruit formation along with the ovary, so it is a false fruit; the guava fruit develops from the ovary after fertilisation, which is why it is taken as a true fruit here.
